02Executive Summary

The task was to denoise the intercepted audio war-intercept.wav, transcribe it, and check the spectrogram for hidden content.

Reading the spectrogram first showed the "noise" was not ambient but seven layers of deliberate, mathematically clean jamming — five steady tones (700/1400/2600/2800/4200 Hz), 60 Hz mains hum, a periodic 1.5 s frequency sweep, an 8 Hz click train and broadband hiss — stacked over speech below ~1 kHz. Each layer was removed with the technique matched to its structure (notches for the tones, a phase-fold tracker for the moving sweep, a voice-aware gate for the clicks, broadband reduction for the hiss), lifting every tone 13–31 dB toward the noise floor while preserving the voice.

Local speech-to-text (Whisper large-v3) then produced a full English transcript at confidence 1.00. The content is not tactical traffic: it is a 1942 radio dramatisation of a US soldier's Christmas letter home, including an acted dinner with Queen Mary — a produced recording used as a decoy. No hidden data was present in the spectrogram. One residual — a faint 8 Hz beat — was shown by testing to be physically irreducible without degrading the voice.

4:39 · 16 kHz mono PCM7 jammer layers13–31 dB tone suppressionEnglish conf 1.000 hidden payloads

04Methodology

Analysis

The file. ffprobe reports a 4 min 39 s (279 s), 16 kHz, mono, 16-bit PCM WAV at 256 kb/s (Step 1). The container's encoder: Lavf63.6.100 tag shows it was assembled with FFmpeg — consistent with a synthetically constructed challenge clip, not a raw field recording. SHA-256 b2e9de27…55d0fd6. All work was performed locally; the audio never left the machine.

Read the spectrogram before filtering. The first action was deliberately not to filter. A spectrogram shows which frequencies are present over time; reading it first reveals the structure of the noise and lets us check whether anyone hid text or an image in the frequencies — which blind denoising would destroy. So the hidden-content check came first.

Hidden-content check — all clear assessed. The original spectrogram was examined at high sensitivity (full band 0–8 kHz, dynamic-range-compressed, plus a zoom). There was no steganographic text, image, SSTV frame or data layer. Supporting checks: LSB distribution noise-like (0.4999); the 7–8 kHz band holds only 0.13% of energy; the tone set does not match the DTMF grid; the file is mono so there is no second-channel payload. The scripted phrase "Perfection Paper Clips" looks like a planted key but is ordinary dialogue (the gift box the narrator reuses). The only engineered structure was the jammer.

The interference is engineered, not ambient proven. A NumPy FFT power-spectrum and envelope autocorrelation (Step 3) pin each layer to exact values:

ComponentMeasurement (measured from the samples)Status
Steady tonesnarrowband peaks at 700, 1400, 2600, 2800, 4200 Hz — measured 695.3 / 1400.4 / 2599.6 / 2799.8 / 4200.2 Hz; a 700 Hz harmonic family (2800 = 4×, 4200 = 6×) plus an independent 2600 Hz tone. Levels −1 to −13 dB (2600 Hz strongest).proven
Mains hum~60 Hz + 120 Hz harmonic (measured 59.6 / 120.1 Hz).proven
Pulse / click traina broadband burst every exactly 125 ms (8 Hz) — autocorrelation peak at 125.0 ms, correlation 0.963, ≈2,200 bursts over 279 s.proven
Frequency sweepa triangle-wave chirp ~1227–4078 Hz, period exactly 1.5000 s (phase-fold residual 0.0 Hz).proven
Speechvoiced energy concentrated below ~1 kHz, intermittent throughout.proven
Table 1 — Jammer components, measured directly from the audio.

Assessment (safe): the exact harmonic frequencies and the exact 125 ms / 1.5000 s periods do not occur in natural noise, so the interference was added deliberately to obscure the speech — layered jamming. The regularity is proven; that it is deliberate is a very safe assessment. assessed

Finding

Speech-to-text (Whisper large-v3, local, Step 5) detected English at confidence 1.00. The content is not tactical traffic — no coordinates, callsigns, frequencies or orders. It is a WWII-era radio dramatisation of a US soldier's Christmas letter home, headed "England, 30 December 1942," signed "Charlie," with an acted scene in which two American officers — Captain Charles Baddeley and Lieutenant Sam Brush — are invited to Christmas dinner with Queen Mary. transcript proven names assessed (degraded audio)

Outcome

  1. Denoising succeeded (proven). The tones, hum and gliding sweep were removed (Table 2); the speech is clearly audible and fully machine-transcribable end to end.
  2. Transcription succeeded (proven). A full English transcript was produced locally (above).
  3. The intercept is a produced radio / entertainment recording, not genuine classified traffic (assessed, high confidence). Scripted actors, sound effects, a 1942 Christmas letter and a dinner with Queen Mary indicate a public recording used as a decoy; the "war intercept" label and the added jamming are decoy framing. The real exercise was signal cleanup and transcription.
  4. The residual 8 Hz beat is irreducible without damaging the voice (proven by testing). It is a train of random broadband bursts fused onto the speech — it can be attenuated (25%, Table 2) but not subtracted. Established by a 10-method tournament plus an ML model (Appendix B). The chosen master keeps the voice natural.
The correct first move on a "noisy intercept" is to read the spectrogram before filtering — to see structure and any hidden content — then remove noise by type rather than with one blunt filter, and to recognise when a residual is physically irreducible rather than over-processing the speech to chase it.

05Step-by-step process (with screenshots)

Step 1 — Inspect the file

Establish exactly what the artefact is before touching it.

ffprobe war-intercept.wav

Step 2 — Image the spectrogram and check for hidden content

Render a spectrogram and inspect it at high sensitivity before filtering. This both reveals the jammer structure and confirms nothing is hidden in the frequencies (see Analysis). The result is Figure 1.

ffmpeg -i war-intercept.wav -lavfi showspectrumpic=s=1180x360:scale=log:legend=1 spec.png

Step 3 — Measure the jammer

Measure the exact tone frequencies and the pulse period straight from the samples with a NumPy FFT (averaged power spectrum) and envelope autocorrelation.

python analyze_jammer.py

Step 4 — Remove each layer, by type

Each jammer layer was removed with the tool matched to its structure (full parameters in Appendix A):

  1. Tones + hum → FFT brick-wall notch (NumPy) at 60/120/700/1400/2600/2800/4200 Hz → intermediate tone_removed.wav. A pure tone is one frequency; a deep narrow null removes it while speech (spread across all frequencies) barely notices.
  2. Sweep → phase-fold median tracker (NumPy STFT, N=512, hop=128, band 450–5100 Hz). Period refined to 1.500 s; ~186 cycles folded into a 360-bin median template; a phase-locked Gaussian notch (depth 0.997, ±90 Hz tracking) follows the moving tone and the signal is rebuilt by overlap-add.
  3. Pulse → voice-activity-aware per-pulse gate (NumPy): period P = 2000 samples (125 ms); a ~100 ms speech envelope vs its median decides gain — soft under speech, deep in the silent gaps.
  4. Hiss + levelling → FFmpeg afftdn, lowpass 3600, dynaudnorm.

Final master: challenge3_output\war-intercept_cleaned.wav. The recovered signal, opened in Audacity:

Step 5 — Transcribe locally

Run Whisper large-v3 on the cleaned audio, offline. PyAV's file decoder is incompatible in this environment, so the audio is decoded to a float32 array and passed to the model; beam_size=5, language English, vad_filter=False (VAD was discarding quiet speech).

python transcribe.py war-intercept_cleaned.wav --model large-v3
In-depth appendices — background and depth beyond the required sections

AAppendix A — The mathematics and parameters

Each layer has a different structure, so each needs a different operation. This is why one "noise-reduction" slider fails — it removes the voice along with the noise.

Y[k] = 0 for k ≈ ftN/fs
Notch the tones. A pure tone occupies one FFT bin; zeroing a thin slot at each tone frequency removes it, while speech spread across all bins is barely affected.
fn = n·f0, f0 = 700 Hz
Harmonic family. 2800 = 4·700 and 4200 = 6·700 — the tones share one generator, evidence of a single synthetic source rather than ambient noise.
S̄(f,φ) = medianc|STFT|(f,φ+cT), T=1.5 s
Fold & trace the sweep. The sweep repeats exactly every T=1.5 s. Folding ~186 cycles and taking the median recovers its moving path while the aperiodic speech averages out; a notch then follows that path. STFT N=512 (32 ms), hop=128 (8 ms), 360 phase bins, Gaussian notch depth 0.997.
r(τ) = Σn e[n]e[n+τ] → peak τ=125 ms
Find the beat. Autocorrelating the high-band envelope e[n] peaks sharply at 125 ms (corr 0.963) — the pulse period is measured, not guessed.
y[n] = g[n]·x[n], g↓ at pulses
Gate the pulses. A time-varying gain g[n] is pulled down on each 125 ms tick — hard in silent gaps, gently under speech (voice-activity-aware, threshold 1.5× the running median) to protect intelligibility.

Why "look first" is mathematically necessary: notching, folding and gating all require parameters — which frequencies, which period, which phase. Those come only from first measuring the signal (Steps 2–3). Filtering before measuring is guessing; measuring first turns each removal into an exact, targeted operation, which is why the voice survives.

BAppendix B — The residual beat: why it cannot be fully removed

The 8 Hz beat is a train of random broadband noise bursts landing at regular times. Consistent noise can be modelled and subtracted; random noise has nothing fixed to subtract, so it can only be attenuated — and because the bursts sit on the same instants as the speech, attenuating hard enough to kill them makes the voice robotic. This was established empirically, not assumed:

MethodWhat it doesOutcome
Per-pulse gate (hard)attenuate each 125 ms tick deeplybeat down, but voice dips → robotic
VAD-aware gate chosensoft under speech, deep in gapsvoice intact; beat partly reduced
De-click (transient)median/impulse repair of clicksvoice consonants dulled; beat partial
HPSS suppressionsplit harmonic vs percussive, cut percussivevoice intact; beat ≈ unchanged
Template subtractionaverage one burst, subtract at each tickfails — bursts are random, no fixed shape
Spectral subtractionestimate noise spectrum, subtractmusical artefacts; voice degraded
Spectral interpolationrepaint burst time-frequency cellsvoice intact; beat partial
AM-flattendivide out the 8 Hz amplitude modulationvoice intact; beat ≈ unchanged (additive, not pure AM)
Narrow notchtreat the beat as a toneno effect — the burst is broadband
ML — MetricGAN+SpeechBrain neural enhancement (PyTorch 2.14)worse — cleaning the background made the bare ticks stand out; voice robotic
Table 3 — Nine DSP methods plus one ML model. All converged on the same wall — the signature of a physical limit, not an un-tuned filter.

CAppendix C — Signal chain & reproducibility

The processing order (each stage's output feeds the next):

war-intercept.wav → [FFT notch: tones+hum] tone_removed.wav → [phase-fold sweep tracker] → [VAD per-pulse gate] → [afftdn · lowpass 3600 · dynaudnorm] → war-intercept_cleaned.wav → [Whisper large-v3] transcript

Deliverables in challenge3_output\: war-intercept_cleaned.wav (voice-first master, SHA-256 a1473d1b…78f927a9), the before/after preview clips, and transcript_narration.txt. All analysis was local; the audio never left the machine. The three terminal screenshots in Step-by-step show these commands run live.

DAppendix D — Anticipated questions

Why look at the spectrogram first?
To see the structure before changing anything — and to check nobody hid data in the frequencies, which blind filtering would destroy.
Why not just use one noise-reduction tool?
The noise was several different types layered together. One blunt filter removes the voice along with the noise; each layer was removed with the tool that fits it.
Why couldn't you remove the beat completely?
It is random noise bursts sitting on the same moments as the speech. Random noise can't be subtracted, only turned down — and turning it down hard makes the voice robotic. Proven with ten methods plus an ML model.
Is this actual classified material?
No. The transcript is a 1940s radio play — a soldier's Christmas letter and a dinner with Queen Mary. A public recording used as a decoy; the jamming was the real test.
How do you know the transcript is right?
The strongest speech-to-text model, run locally on the cleaned audio, returns coherent connected English that matches the story end to end — not random words.

EAppendix E — Glossary

Spectrogram
A picture of a sound: frequency (vertical) against time (horizontal), brightness = energy. Steady tones appear as horizontal lines.
FFT / STFT
Fast Fourier Transform converts a slice of sound into its frequencies; the Short-Time FFT does this on a sliding window to track how frequencies change over time.
Notch filter
A filter that removes a very narrow band of frequencies (here, each jammer tone) while leaving the rest intact.
Phase-fold
Stacking a signal on a known period so repeating content reinforces and non-repeating content (speech) averages out — used to recover the moving sweep.
Autocorrelation
Comparing a signal with a time-shifted copy of itself; a peak at a given lag reveals a repeating period (here, 125 ms).
VAD
Voice-Activity Detection — deciding where speech is present, so the pulse gate can be gentle on the voice and aggressive in the gaps.
LSB steganography
Hiding data in the least-significant bits of audio samples; a uniform bit distribution (0.4999 here) means none is present.
SSTV / DTMF
Slow-Scan TV encodes images as tones; DTMF are telephone keypad tones. Checked for and absent.
dBFS
Decibels relative to full scale — 0 dBFS is the loudest a digital sample can be; more negative is quieter.
